series: Climate Fiscal Policy Briefs, Section 1: Carbon Pricing
title: Price Production and Consumption Separately

slides.title: Price Production and Consumption Separately
slides.subtitle: Carbon pricing in open economies: Briefs 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4 and 6.1
slides.message: Carbon prices stall because one instrument does two jobs. Price production with a revenue-neutral feebate, consumption through VAT and a forward obligation on fuel suppliers, and measure both on one scale.

slides.title: Why carbon prices stall in open economies
slides.text: A tax on domestic production charges exports, which are consumed abroad, and spares imports, which are consumed at home. Exporters lose share, so governments exempt industry and hold the rate down.
points: Job 1, production: reward firms for cutting emissions per unit of output.
Job 2, consumption: make buyers pay for the carbon in what they use, imports included.
CBAM protects the EU market from untaxed imports, but does nothing for exporters and credits only prices paid.

slides.title: The two-track architecture (1.1)
slides.caption: Stylized steel-like sector: e0 = 2 tCO2/t, p0 = $600/t, 30% intensity cut at $50/tCO2.
points: Residual cost: a feebate raises the price $15/t (2.5%); a tax at the same rate, $85/t (14%).
Crediting: a payment above half the feebate rate makes adoption a net gain; best rate = payment.
Race to the top: each exporter's most competitive feebate rate equals the charge in its markets.

slides.title: Feebates: the full price at the margin (1.2)
slides.caption: Change in generation cost per MWh at $50/tCO2, stylized grid of 60% coal: tax against feebate.
points: Fee above a sector benchmark, rebate below; fees fund rebates.
Same merit order and same clean-versus-coal choice as a tax.
India at $50/t: tariff +$1/MWh under a feebate, +$36 under a tax.
Uniform-price wholesale market: +$13/MWh.

slides.title: A consumption tax through VAT (1.4)
slides.caption: Effective VAT rate by embodied-carbon intensity, 2027–2037, stylized path.
points: A carbon component in VAT, imports and EU goods alike; exports zero-rated; rebuttable defaults.
A forward obligation, fixed a decade ahead, on suppliers of fuel for homes and vehicles.
Basket: 0.41 kg CO2e per euro (2022); imports twice EU-made goods.
At €200/t the poorest fifth pays 0.4% of spending more, the richest 0.2% less.

slides.title: CBAM: recognition and scrap shuffling (1.3)
slides.caption: Scrap shuffling in a stylized exporter: routing scrap-based steel to the EU cuts the embodied carbon the border sees.
points: A revenue-neutral feebate charges the full rate at the margin but earns nothing: its average payment is zero.
At €80/t, shuffling saves €100–600 per tonne of steel across thirteen exporters, with no cut in emissions.
Measure by country and sector: shuffling earns nothing; phase in 2027–2034 with relocation reviews.

slides.title: The Total Effective Carbon Price (6.1)
slides.caption: Explicit-price metric and TECP by instrument, stylized three-sector economy.
points: The uniform carbon tax that cuts emissions as much as the policy mix.
Explicit prices: $21/t. TECP: $37/t long run ($32–38), $28 after one year.
A fuel standard at $166/t adds only $1.
Lets a country that regulates earn what one that taxes earns.

slides.title: What to do
todo: Exporters: start with a production feebate, in power first, then steel, cement and aluminum.
EU: recognize the country-sector price signal at the border, feebates included.
EU: put a forward obligation on fuel suppliers now; move part of VAT onto carbon.
Crediting facilities: pay for policies, measured as TECP, above half the feebate rate.
